Seven runs rather than one — the old single line four times, bounded so each run reports which way the race fell, and the published pair three times with nothing between the apply and the wait — then the paused shape, then a third shape neither of us had named. failures.criterion: The sequence's waits must answer about the workload the role just submitted. Re-using the name the section tells a role to use, straight after the `kubectl delete job` the sequence itself ends with, makes both waits answer about the **previous** run's terminating pod: `--for=create` returns on it and `--for=condition=Ready` reports `condition met` for it while the new workload is still Pending.
failures.evidence: Measured at code head 490e525b from this role container as `system:serviceaccount:<legion namespace>:legion-worker`. The shape is the section's own advice followed twice: name the workload for the issue, run the sequence, let it end in `kubectl delete job`, then run it again — which is what a role does after any failure in the middle of it. Observed: the first run reaches Ready and is deleted; the same manifest is applied again at once; `kubectl get pod -l job-name=<workload>` then shows **two** pods, the new one `Pending` and the old one `Terminating`, because a terminating pod keeps the `job-name` label; `kubectl wait --for=create pod -l job-name=<workload>` returns 0 after 1 s — on the dying pod; and `kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l job-name=<workload> --timeout=300s` prints `pod/<the previous run's pod> condition met` and exits 0 after 2 s, while the pod that will serve is still Pending. The sequence then runs its reachability check and its `kubectl logs` against a workload that is not up, and a role reading a timeout there is sent by the section to the reachability label — the one failure it says announces nothing. This is the original defect's shape rather than a new one: a wait that answers about the wrong thing, reachable now through the line that fixed the first. The Ready wait behaved this way before this round too; what is new is that `--for=create` also returns on the stale pod, so the pair gives a role two reasons to believe a workload is up when it is not. No red test is possible for a sequence on a page, so the evidence is the run above; the remedies are each one line — wait for the old pod to go (`kubectl wait --for=delete pod -l job-name=<workload> --timeout=120s` before the apply), or wait on the Job rather than on a label (`kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready job/<workload>`), or select the new pod by the uid the sequence already reads.
failures.criterionSource: a third shape of my own, invited by the section's own naming rule and its own last command; it meets the architect's bar — a statement that would make a reader do the wrong thing — rather than the child-issue bar

proof.criterion: The race the two waits were added for: the published pair closes it, and it closes it in the shape where the gap is wide and in the shape where it hides.
proof.surface: This role container against the live namespace, seven runs, each bounded and deleted by hand.
proof.command: the old single `kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l job-name=… --timeout=5s` immediately after the apply, four times, the short timeout telling which way the race fell ; then the published pair (`--for=create` then Ready) immediately after the apply, three times ; then the pair with a ten-second pause standing in for the Service steps
proof.observed: The race is real and it is a coin: of four runs of the old single line, two lost it outright — `error: no matching resources found`, exit 1 at once — one found the pod and timed out at its five seconds as a wait should, and one found the pod already Ready. So the old line fails about half the time here, which is exactly why one run of it proves nothing either way. The published pair closes it: `--for=create` returned 0 after 0 s, 1 s and 1 s in the three no-pause runs, and the paused shape behaved identically (create at 11 s, Ready at 11 s on a warm machine), with Postgres's own `database system is ready to accept connections` in the log afterwards. I ran the no-pause shape first and more often than the paused one, for the reason the architect named: a wait that merely polled would pass the paused case and fail the other, so the wide-gap run is the one that can disprove the fix.
proof.negativeControl: The control is the old line at this same head, in the same shape, with the same image and node: it is what loses the race two times in four while the pair never did in four runs. `kubectl version` here is v1.35.9, so `--for=create` is a verb this image's client has rather than one the page assumes.

observations: The finding above does not live inside this round's fix in the sense of being caused by it: the Ready wait has always answered on whatever the label selected, and a terminating pod has always kept that label. What this round changed is that the new `--for=create` line answers on the stale pod too, so where a role once had one misleading answer it now has two. The fix for the first race is right and I would keep it; it needs one more line beside it.

The race's own numbers are worth keeping for whoever reads this later: the old single line lost two times in four here, which is why the implementer could write it, run it once, and see it work. That is the shape of this whole issue in one measurement.
